newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican lawmakers mull "certifying" U.S. for drugs.
newsitem.headline: Mexican lawmakers mull "certifying" U.S. for drugs.

text.p: Mexican senators have proposed a law that would require Mexico to "certify" U.S. anti-drug efforts in the same way the United States cerfifies the efforts of other nations in the drug war.

The move follows an angry war of words between lawmakers in both countries over last week's move by President Bill Clinton to certify that Mexico is an ally in the drug war, despite recent drug corruption scandals in Mexico.

"It is a bill that would certify the anti-drug efforts of other countries with whom we cooperate or who also put us to test," said Fernando Solana, a former foreign minister and head of the Mexican Senate's foreign affairs committee.

Mexico complained bitterly that the certification process interferes with its internal affairs and defended its anti-drugs record, despite the embarrassing recent arrest of its top anti-drugs official on drug corruption charges.
Although the Clinton administration certified Mexico, a U.S. House of Representatives committee voted on Thursday to revoke the ratification, meaning the full House would have to vote on the measure.

The move elicited angry responses on Friday from Mexican lawmakers and even prompted a masked Mexican social activist known as SuperBarrio to jokingly "certify" the United States as the world's top drug consumer.

Solana, a member of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party, said the United States has been pressing Mexico to allow more U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency agents to operate here, to carry weapons and to have certain police powers.
"There are some proposals the United States has made that are unacceptable... In no way will we accept these," Solana said in the interview with Televisa television network.
